usage: the default verb is 끓이다 'boil', not 만들다 'make'; you boil water and add the noodle block
붇다 (ㄷ-irregular → 불어요) is the specific verb for noodles swelling and going soft if you wait too long; do not confuse it with 불다 'to blow'
봉지 'bag/packet' counts the sealed package; 개 also works informally
prefix-style compound: instant ramen in a cup you just add hot water to
examples: 저는 라면을 좋아해요.
I like ramen.
simple statement of preference with 을 marking the object
밤에 라면을 끓여 먹으면 너무 맛있어요.
Ramen tastes so good when you cook and eat it at night.
끓여 먹다 'boil-and-eat' is the natural verb chain; note the late-night-snack culture
면 다 붇기 전에 빨리 드세요.
Eat quickly before the noodles get all soggy.
real-table urgency; 면 = noodles, base verb 붇다 keeps ㄷ before the consonant ending 기 (붇기), 드세요 is the polite imperative
nuance: 라면 to a Korean means the cheap instant noodle block you boil at home in a small pot (양은냄비), eaten with kimchi at midnight — it is comfort food and student food, not a restaurant meal. The crucial dividing line is 라면 vs 라멘: 라멘 is the Japanese-restaurant bowl with rich tonkotsu/miso broth and chashu, while 라면 is the supermarket packet (신라면, 진라면). The word came in from Japanese ラーメン (itself from Chinese 拉麵 'pulled noodles'), but in Korea it shifted to mean the instant version specifically. Register is fully casual and neutral — anyone says it. The collocation trap: you 끓이다 'boil' ramen, you do not 만들다 'make' it, and the noodles 붇다 'swell/go soggy' (ㄷ-irregular → 불어요/불었어요, but 붇기 before a consonant) rather than 'get wet' — note 붇다 is a different verb from 불다 'to blow'. English speakers also wrongly assume 라면 covers fancy ramen-shop noodles; for that you must say 라멘.

Using 라면 to mean the Japanese ramen-shop dish — that is 라멘. Mixing them up makes a Korean picture a supermarket packet, not a restaurant bowl.
Describing soggy noodles as 라면이 젖었어요 ('the ramen got wet') — the correct verb is 불었어요 (from the ㄷ-irregular base 붇다, not 불다 'to blow'), the specific word for noodles swelling and softening.

usage: the verb is 싸다 'wrap', because you roll the rice and fillings in seaweed; not 만들다 for the rolling act
줄 'line/strip' is the proper counter for a whole long roll; one 줄 is cut into bite pieces
compound naming by filling: 참치 'tuna' + 김밥; menus list 야채김밥, 치즈김밥 the same way
the famous cheap chain; shows 김밥 as everyday fast food you grab on the go
examples: 김밥 한 줄 주세요.
One roll of gimbap, please.
ordering at a shop; note the counter 줄, never 개, for a whole roll
소풍 갈 때 엄마가 김밥을 싸 주셨어요.
When we went on a picnic, my mom rolled gimbap for us.
싸 주다 'roll for someone' + honorific 주셨어요; picnic-and-gimbap is a core memory
김밥은 식어도 맛있어서 들고 다니기 좋아요.
Gimbap is tasty even cold, so it is great to carry around.
real reasoning with -아서; explains why it is the go-to portable food
nuance: 김밥 is steamed rice and fillings (egg, pickled radish, carrot, spinach, ham) rolled in dried laver and sliced into bite-size pieces — cheap, portable, the definitive picnic and lunchbox food. The name transparently combines 김 'dried laver/seaweed' + 밥 'rice', so a learner can decode it. Do not confuse it with Japanese 김초밥/마키(스시): gimbap rice is seasoned with sesame oil and salt, not vinegar, and the fillings are cooked, so it is its own dish, not 'Korean sushi' (Koreans dislike that label). Two collocation points trip up English speakers: you 싸다 'wrap/roll' gimbap (the rolling motion), not 만들다; and you count a whole roll with 줄 'strip', so '두 줄' = two rolls, while 개 would wrongly count individual slices. Register is casual and universal.

mistakes: Counting whole rolls with 개 — 김밥 두 개 sounds like two single slices. Use 줄: 김밥 두 줄 = two rolls.
Calling it 'Korean sushi' or equating it with 초밥 — the rice uses sesame oil and salt (not vinegar) and the fillings are cooked, so it is a distinct dish; many Koreans find the sushi comparison off.
Saying 김밥을 만들어요 for the act of rolling — the idiomatic verb is 싸다 (싸요), as in 김밥을 싸요, because you are wrapping/rolling it.

usage: the matching verb 비비다 'mix/rub' shares the root of the noun; you stir everything before eating
고추장 is the signature sauce; 넣다 'put in' is how you add it before mixing
compound: 돌솥 'stone pot' + 비빔밥, served sizzling so the bottom rice crisps
그릇 'bowl' is the natural counter for served rice dishes
examples: 저는 비빔밥을 좋아해요.
I like bibimbap.
plain preference; 을 marks the object
고추장 넣고 잘 비벼서 드세요.
Add the chili paste and mix it well before eating.
real serving instruction; 비벼서 (from 비비다) + 드세요, the polite imperative
채소가 많아서 비빔밥은 건강한 한 끼예요.
Because it has lots of vegetables, bibimbap is a healthy meal.
reasoning with -아서; 한 끼 'one meal' frames it as a full, balanced meal
nuance: 비빔밥 is a bowl of warm rice topped with seasoned vegetables (나물), often an egg and a little meat, plus 고추장 chili paste, all stirred together right before eating. The name is pure native Korean and self-explaining: it is 비비다 'to mix/rub' turned into the noun 비빔 + 밥 'rice', literally 'mixed rice'. The whole point is the mixing, which sets up the key collocation 비비다 — you 비벼서 먹다 'mix-and-eat', and a learner who eats it in neat layers has missed the dish. Distinguish it from 덮밥 'rice topped with something' (a 덮밥 you eat as-is, scooping topping with rice; a 비빔밥 you must stir). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 섞다 'to mix' — 섞다 is for blending separate substances (mixing flour and water), but for stirring food in a bowl with utensils the idiomatic verb is 비비다. Register is neutral and everyday.

Forgetting the object particle in casual speech and over-correcting to 가/이 — it is 비빔밥을 먹어요/비벼요 (object 을), since the rice is what you act on.

usage: 재우다 'let it rest/soak' is the cooking term for marinating the beef in sauce before grilling
양념 'seasoning mix'; 불고기 is defined by its sweet 간장(soy) base, unlike spicy dishes
백반-style set: 불고기 with rice and side dishes at a restaurant
굽다 'grill/roast'; note it is a ㅂ-irregular, so 굽다 → 구워요
examples: 저는 불고기를 좋아해요.
I like bulgogi.
simple preference; 를 marks the object after a vowel
오늘 저녁에 불고기를 먹고 싶어요.
I want to eat bulgogi tonight.
-고 싶다 'want to'; a very natural dinner wish
불고기는 양념이 달아서 아이들도 잘 먹어요.
Bulgogi has a sweet marinade, so even kids eat it well.
reasoning with -아서; explains why this mild, sweet meat is family-friendly
nuance: 불고기 is thin slices of beef marinated in a sweet soy-sauce mix (간장, sugar, garlic, sesame oil, often pear or onion) and grilled or pan-cooked, giving a tender, sweet-savory result rather than charred plain meat. The name is native Korean and decodes literally as 불 'fire' + 고기 'meat', i.e. 'fire-meat'. The sharpest contrast is 불고기 vs 갈비/삼겹살: 갈비 is short rib (also marinated, on the bone), 삼겹살 is fatty pork belly grilled plain and dipped after, while 불고기 is sliced, pre-marinated, sweet. So 불고기 is not a generic word for 'grilled meat' — that broader idea is 구이 or 고기구이. Collocation note for English speakers: you 재우다 'marinate' (let it soak) the meat, and you 굽다 'grill' it (ㅂ-irregular: 구워요). The pitfall is assuming any Korean BBQ meat is 불고기; if it is unmarinated pork belly it is 삼겹살, not 불고기. Register is neutral, used by everyone.

Conjugating 굽다 'grill' as regular (구버요) — it is ㅂ-irregular, so the correct form is 구워요 (불고기를 구워요).
Calling the sauce 소스 — the marinade for Korean meat is 양념, and 불고기 is 양념 고기 (seasoned meat); 소스 sounds like a Western dipping sauce.

usage: 인분 'portion per person'; street tteokbokki is sold by the serving, not by piece
맵다 'spicy' (ㅂ-irregular → 매워요); spiciness is its defining trait
compound by style: 국물 'broth' version with more sauce to drink/dip in
볶다 'stir-fry' is the root verb; the cakes are cooked down in the sauce
examples: 저는 떡볶이를 좋아해요.
I like tteokbokki.
plain preference statement
분식집에서 떡볶이 일 인분 주세요.
One serving of tteokbokki at the snack shop, please.
real ordering; 분식집 = snack bar, counter 인분 for the serving
떡볶이가 너무 매워서 물을 많이 마셨어요.
The tteokbokki was so spicy that I drank a lot of water.
cause-result with -아서; 맵다 → 매워서 (ㅂ-irregular)
nuance: 떡볶이 is chewy cylindrical rice cakes (떡) simmered in a sweet-spicy 고추장 red sauce, the iconic 분식 (snack-shop) street food eaten by students after school. The name is native Korean: 떡 'rice cake' + 볶이 from 볶다 'to stir-fry', so literally 'stir-fried rice cakes' (even though it is now more simmered than fried). The key collocation is the adjective 맵다 'spicy', a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 매워요/매워서 — spiciness is the whole identity of the dish, so expecting it to be sweet-only is the beginner's surprise. It is counted by 인분 'serving per person', not by individual cakes. Contrast 떡볶이 with plain 떡 (rice cake), which can be a chewy sweet snack like 가래떡; 떡볶이 specifically means the saucy spicy dish. English-speaker pitfall: do not call it 'rice cake' alone in a food context — that suggests the unseasoned 떡 or even a Western rice cracker; the dish is always the full word 떡볶이. Register is casual and youthful.

usage: 시키다 'order (in)' is the go-to verb; 치킨 culture is built on delivery 배달
마리 counts whole animals; a full order is one 마리, half is 반 마리
compound: 양념 'seasoning' + 치킨; the saucy variety vs plain 후라이드
blend of 치킨 + 맥주; the beloved fried-chicken-with-beer combo
examples: 저는 치킨을 좋아해요.
I like fried chicken.
simple preference
오늘 저녁에 치킨 한 마리 시킬까요?
Shall we order a whole chicken for dinner tonight?
-(으)ㄹ까요 suggestion; 시키다 for delivery, counter 마리
치킨은 역시 맥주랑 같이 먹어야 맛있어요.
Fried chicken really tastes best when you eat it with beer.
역시 'as expected' + -아야 '(must/should)'; the 치맥 ritual
nuance: 치킨 in Korea means deep-fried (or sauced) chicken that you order for delivery and share with friends or family over beer — a whole social ritual, not just a food. It is an English loanword (chicken), but its meaning narrowed: 치킨 = fried chicken the dish, while the live bird or raw meat is 닭 'chicken' / 닭고기 'chicken meat'. This is the central pitfall for English speakers: '닭/닭고기' for the ingredient, '치킨' only for the cooked fried dish — saying 치킨 for raw chicken in a recipe is wrong. Key collocations: you 시키다 'order' it (delivery culture), count it with 마리 (whole animal, so 한 마리 / 반 마리), and pair it as 치맥 (치킨+맥주). Contrast 후라이드(치킨) 'plain fried' vs 양념(치킨) 'sweet-spicy sauced' — the classic 'half-and-half' is 반반. Register is fully casual and ubiquitous.

usage: 빚다 'shape by hand' is the artisanal verb for folding dumplings (also used for 송편, pottery)
prefix by method: 군- (from 굽다 'fry') + 만두; cf. 찐만두 steamed, 물만두 boiled-in-water
개 counts individual dumplings; a plate/order may use 접시 or 인분
만두 in broth (note the 사이시옷: 만두+국 → 만둣국), a New Year dish with 떡국
examples: 저는 만두를 좋아해요.
I like dumplings.
plain preference; no plural ending in Korean
설날에 가족이 모여서 만두를 빚어요.
On New Year's Day the family gathers and folds dumplings.
빚다 'fold/shape'; the communal New Year tradition
군만두는 바삭하고 물만두는 부드러워요.
Pan-fried dumplings are crispy and water-boiled ones are soft.
contrasting cooking methods with -고; shows the prefix system
nuance: 만두 are dough pockets filled with minced meat, tofu, vegetables, and glass noodles, which can be steamed (찐만두), pan-fried (군만두), or boiled in soup (물만두/만둣국) — one word covering all methods, so you prefix the style. It is Sino-Korean, written 饅頭 (literally 'steamed bun/stuffed head'), a word shared across East Asia. A learner should not equate it narrowly with Japanese 'gyoza': 교자(만두) is the thin-skinned pan-fried type, but 만두 is the broad category, including thick-skinned and soup versions. The grammar pitfall is the strongest one: Korean nouns are not pluralized, so 'dumplings' is still just 만두 (never 만두들 here) — you say 만두를 먹어요 for any number. The signature verb is 빚다 'to shape/fold by hand' (the same verb used for shaping 송편 rice cakes), which is more idiomatic than 만들다 for the folding craft. Register is neutral and everyday.

usage: 쑤다 is the dedicated verb for cooking porridge/paste; more precise than 끓이다 or 만들다
compound by ingredient: 전복 'abalone' + 죽; also 호박죽 pumpkin, 닭죽 chicken
그릇 'bowl' is the counter; porridge is served and eaten by the bowl
먹다 'eat' (with a spoon), not 마시다 'drink', even though it is liquidy
examples: 저는 죽을 좋아해요.
I like porridge.
plain preference statement
감기에 걸려서 죽을 먹었어요.
I caught a cold, so I ate porridge.
cause with -아서; 죽 as the classic sick-day comfort food
할머니가 전복죽을 쑤어 주셨어요.
Grandma made abalone porridge for me.
쑤다 'cook porridge' + honorific 주셨어요; warmth and care
nuance: 죽 is a soft, slow-simmered rice porridge eaten when you are sick, recovering, or want something gentle on the stomach — culturally it carries a strong 'comfort / convalescence / care' feeling, so bringing someone 죽 signals concern. It is Sino-Korean, written 粥 'congee/gruel'. Distinguish it along a thickness scale: 미음 is the thinnest (strained, for the very ill or babies), 죽 is the standard porridge, and 누룽지 is the toasted scorched-rice version — so 죽 is the middle, everyday term. please give me more side dishes

usage: 먹다 'eat'; a light bite between meals to tide you over
시간 'time'; the set snack break, especially for children at school/home
-거리 'stuff/material for'; 간식거리 = snack items, things to nibble
으로 marks 'as/for' a snack; names what the snack is
examples: 저는 간식을 좋아해요.
I like snacks.
simple preference statement
배고픈데 간식 좀 먹을까요?

-는데 'since/and' background + -ㄹ까요 suggestion; everyday offer
아이들 간식으로 과일을 준비했어요.

nuance: 간식 is a light snack eaten between meals to bridge hunger — fruit, rice cakes, cookies, bread — never a full meal in itself. It is Sino-Korean, written 間食, literally 'between (間) + eating (食)', i.e. 'eating in between', which pinpoints its meaning: food taken in the gap between regular meals. This sets up a precise three-way contrast you should master: 간식 = between-meal snack, 후식 (後食) = dessert right after a meal, 야식 (夜食) = late-night food. They are not interchangeable — fruit eaten at 3 p.m. is 간식, the same fruit eaten right after dinner is 후식, and fried chicken at midnight is 야식. The English-speaker pitfall is using 간식 for any non-main food including dessert; keep 간식 strictly for the between-meals bite and use 후식 for the end-of-meal sweet. Culturally, 간식 strongly evokes children's snack time. Register is neutral and everyday.

usage: 먹다 'eat'; the sweet course taken right after the main meal

I like dessert.
plain preference statement

nuance: 후식 is dessert — the sweet or finishing course eaten right after a meal, such as fruit, ice cream, tteok, or coffee. It is Sino-Korean, written 後食, literally 'after (後) + eating (食)', i.e. 'after-food', so the etymology directly encodes 'what you eat after the meal'. The key synonym pair is 후식 vs 디저트: they mean the same thing, but 후식 is the native Sino-Korean term that feels slightly more traditional/formal (a set-menu 'course' served as 후식), while 디저트 is the English loanword that dominates café culture and trendy sweets — you order 디저트 at a dessert café, but a Korean restaurant's set meal lists 후식. The sharp contrast to drill is 후식 (after-meal dessert) vs 간식 (間食, between-meals snack): an apple after lunch is 후식; an apple at 3 p.m. between meals is 간식. The English-speaker pitfall is lumping all sweet snacks as 'dessert/후식' — Korean separates the end-of-meal course (후식) from the between-meal nibble (간식). Register is neutral.
